**CFTC and ETF Report** _A weekly update of futures and exchange traded fund activity._ • Gold looked in reasonably good shape when our last CFTC report was published. The $100 drop at the end of February was a receding memory, and many in the market perceived the recovery to $1,700 (which took prices back above the 200 day moving average) as evidence of longstanding gold bulls gradually rebuilding the positions that had been liquidated. This proved to be a false dawn, however: each successive piece of positive US economic data dealt a fresh blow to the hopes of those who still clung to the possibility of QE3 as gold’s salvation, while the Eurozone debt worries that had stimulated some safe-haven demand for the yellow metal were quickly fading. Without these props in place, longs lacked confidence that gold could move much further above $1,700 in the short term. • The silver price largely followed the gold price last week. The recovery above $34.00 barely survived the first Asian session of the week and by the middle of the week silver had plummeted below $31.65. The modest improvement in user demand that followed the big move down at the end of February is still present, but alone is insufficient to support the price above $34.00 at present. We will need to se a major resurgence in investment demand if silver is to regain a solid footing above current levels. • The first day of last week saw platinum finally recapture its premium over gold. Gold had maintained the upper hand since September 2011 but recent macro pressure on the yellow metal alongside concerns over possible disruptions to South Africa’s platinum mines set the spread on course to narrow sooner rather than later. Moreover the fact that the main drivers behind the selloff in gold were specifically bearish gold rather than generally bearish precious metals have meant that platinum has been far more resilient in recent weeks. When gold lost 4.7% last week platinum lost only 2.4% and swiftly recovered. A bout of heavy selling on Friday morning however meant that platinum ended the week down $15, which still compares favourably with gold’s loss of $50. **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **19 March 2012** #### **New York:** 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 #### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 #### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 #### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 #### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | CFTC and ETF Weekly Report** **19 March 2012** ## **Gold CFTC data to 13 March 2012; ETF data to 16 March 2012.** |**Exchang**|**e (COMEX a**

en March 6th—13th. Any change of less than about half a million ounces is very small by gold’s standards, but after the combined 6.2 million ounce liquidation seen across Comex and Tocom during the previous week there was clearly not much length in the market left to be washed out. Next week’s figures should give us a clearer impression of where investor sentiment currently stands. - Gold ETF flows were even more unremarkable, with just 5,800 ounces of net inflows globally. - The silver price largely followed the gold price last week. The recovery above $34.00 barely survived the first Asian session of the week and by the middle of the week silver had plummeted below $31.65. As is so often the case, the move in silver was an amplification of the move in gold: while gold lost 4.7% from March 12-14, silver lost 7.9%. The modest improvement in user demand that followed the big move down at the end of February is still present, but alone is insufficient to support the price above $34.00 at present. We will need to se a major resurgence in

investment demand if silver is to regain a solid footing above current levels. - Like in gold, the enormous liquidation (over 50 million ounces) seen in silver in the week preceding our last report meant that there was not too much length remaining to be trimmed. A decrease of 6.9 million ounces in large long Comex futures positioning was almost completely offset by increases in small longs and in options positions. - Silver ETFs reduced their holdings by an unremarkable 620,000 ounces between March 9th— 16th. ZKB and iShares silver—two of the largest silver ETFs—were jointly responsible for virtually all of the selling as other major funds kept holdings unchanged. - Palladium last week t

raded in a familiar range straddling $700. $709 provided a firm ceiling while buying interest was rejuvenated on the odd dip below $695. Price action was choppy despite this narrow range, and the low and the high of the week were both made on a $20 move within a three hour spell on Thursday afternoon. 

- Net long speculative positions in palladium increased between March 6th—13th, setting it apart from the other precious metals during the same period. Overall long positioning increased by an impressive 118,000 ounces, the overwhelming majority of which was accounted for by increases in large specs on Nymex. 

- While gold ETFs added barely anything to metal holdings and silver and platinum ETFs reduced, last week saw palladium ETFs add more than 28,000 ounces. Another week of solid inflows brings this year’s total additions across palladium ETFs to more than 240,000 ounces. By comparison, platinum ETFs have added just 102,000 ounces in the same period. The Nymex figures and ETF figures together suggest that palladium is enjoying a rare moment of pre-eminence in the favours of investors.
